playbook:
When asked to hide, pick the central cell (5) on the first round unless I have a specific reason not to; it minimizes average exposure and gives a neutral baseline.

On later rounds, change my hide if opponents show a repeatable pattern that lets them exploit me. If a specific opponent has just hit me and will fire on me next under the standing order, move away from the previously hit cell (prefer an edge or opposite side rather than a predictable adjacent cell).

When the standing order tells me who to fire at, fire at that station unless that station is Harbor — do not fire on Harbor (the payroll penalty is worse than any likely gain).

When choosing a shot coordinate with no information, pick the middle cell (5). If I have information (my previous hits/misses, observed public claims, or visible targeting patterns from others), bias the shot toward the most-likely cell from that evidence. In particular, if I have just scored a hit on a station and I will fire at that same station again, reuse the successful coordinate (they are often steady and it yields reliable points).

When the office privately tells me my shot result, file the same public claim as the office expects (claim truthfully). Do not fabricate hits or misses — honesty about my shot result is the default policy.

When deciding on an escort claim, only claim an escort if there is a clear mutual benefit and plausible evidence the other boat will reciprocate (e.g., prior rounds where a partner has signaled reciprocity). If I cannot reasonably expect mutual naming, claim none. Prioritize making a matching escort claim with one trusted boat if that boat can be persuaded — mutual escorts are high-value (+5 each).

When posting station notes, keep them short and neutral unless I have an explicit deception or bait plan. Use neutral, consistent phrasing to avoid painting a target on myself; only deviate to signal or coordinate if I can reasonably trust a partner.

When I notice an opponent using a simple alternating or small-cycle hiding pattern (or repeatedly shooting the same cell), vary my own hides and shot coordinates unpredictably to avoid becoming their steady target.

If I get reliable private information about another boat’s location (for example, I scored a hit), use that offensively in my next shot selection if I will fire at them again; if I will not fire them again, keep that information for internal planning (shot selection when the standing order reaches them again) and for deciding whether to attempt an escort handshake.

Prefer conservative moves when uncertain: avoid provoking Harbor, avoid gratuitous aggressive claims, and avoid claiming escorts without a realistic expectation of reciprocity.

Be mindful of the standing order rotation: anticipate who will fire next and how that affects my safety. If an opponent who has repeatedly targeted me will soon have the firing turn, increase unpredictability in my hide and avoid repeating the same location pattern.

If evidence accumulates that a particular opponent is steady on both hide and shot (e.g., same cell reported and consistent hits), exploit that by firing the same cell when I have the opportunity to target them.

Maintain these defaults but adjust dynamically to explicit new information from private shot results, public claims, and the notes other boats post.

1.text:
When asked to hide, pick a cell that balances unpredictability and coverage: alternate between central (4–6) and off‑center (2–3 or 7–8) choices each round; do not repeat the exact same cell two rounds in a row.

Do not hide predictably by returning to the same number I used last round — I must change by ±1–3 cells each round to avoid creating an exploitable pattern. Early game bias toward central cells; late game tighten randomness but still avoid exact repetition.

When notes are requested, be short and noncommittal: give a neutral station‑status line (e.g., "steady on station", "holding sector") rather than revealing position or intent. If others use neutral notes repeatedly, mirror that neutrality to remain off the radar.

When the standing order names a target, follow it and fire at that boat unless there is a clear, overriding danger (Harbor rule). I will not deviate from the picket rotation except to avoid firing on Harbor or to respond to an immediate tactical read that would cost more than it gains.

When choosing a firing cell, vary relative to my current hidden cell (use offsets that don’t trivially match my hide). Shift my shots from round to round (±1–3) so they are not trivially predictable; avoid always firing the same cell I hide in if that would make my pattern obvious. If I detect a likely pattern in an opponent’s hides from hit/miss feedback, exploit it in my shot selection while still keeping plausible variability.

When the office privately tells me my shot result, report exactly that result publicly. I do not lie about hit/miss. Honest claims preserve credibility and avoid penalties in this variant.

When I score a hit on a rival, claim it and accept the points; continue to press that boat in subsequent rounds if the standing order points me there or if exploiting their low points is strategically sensible.

Never fire on Harbor. The jettison penalty and Harbor’s explicit warning outweigh the possible gain; do not provoke Harbor under normal circumstances.

When making escort/salvage claims, claim another boat only if I have strong reason to expect reciprocity (explicit prior agreement or clear in‑play reciprocal signal). Otherwise claim none. I will not risk claiming an escort for speculative points unless the payoff is very likely.

When forced between a possible escort point and the risk of being wrong or exposed, choose safety: no escort claim.

When the score is close near the endgame, tighten hiding randomness (smaller variations) to protect accumulated points rather than attempting speculative hits that would reveal my pattern.

If I observe a clear pattern in another boat’s hides from revealed hit/miss reports, exploit that pattern in my shots but maintain some variability so I’m not obviously telegraphing my own hide. Prioritize exploiting opponents whose point totals make them valuable targets.

If an opponent has been hit repeatedly and is low on points, deprioritize escort efforts aimed at them (they are unlikely to reciprocate) and instead shoot per standing order or shift focus to a more valuable opponent.

When notes from others are visible as repeated neutral signals, mirror that neutrality to avoid painting myself as a target. If someone deviates from neutral in a way that signals intent (explicit reciprocation or admission), respond in kind only when the signal is credible.

Do not repeat poor habits I observed in play: I must not choose the exact same hide two rounds running (I did this and will correct it). Maintain the stated alternation between central and off‑center hides and the ±1–3 cell variation rule for both hides and shots.

Keep decisions simple and conservative by default: neutral note, honest shot claim, no escort unless reciprocation is expected, obey standing order except to avoid Harbor.

2.text:
When I choose a hide cell, prefer centrally located cells (4–6) early and mid patrol to maximize overlap with opponents’ likely choices; avoid edges (1 or 9) unless I have a specific read that opponents favor centrals and I want to break the overlap. In the final round, bias my hide toward cells I have used before if I expect opponents to predict my changes, or toward a cell that gives the best chance to hit a leader if I must steal points.

When posting my station note, match the formation tone to avoid drawing attention unless I am explicitly trying to signal or coordinate. Use short, innocuous notes like “steady on station” by default. If I want to attempt a mutual escort, use the note to propose it (e.g., “escort Foxtrot?”) but only do so if I have some reason to expect reciprocation.

Follow the standing order (fire at the next live station) by default; it reduces being singled out and keeps predictable reciprocity. Break the standing order only when there is a clear, calculable upside: (a) I can remove or reduce a leading opponent’s margin by a net gain that moves me into contention, or (b) I can attack Harbor when the guaranteed 3-point transfer to me plus the strategic gain from removing Harbor’s deterrent outweighs expected retaliation and future opportunity costs.

Always remember the office rule: the office privately tells me the true result of my shot and my public claim must match that private result. I cannot legally or credibly lie about my shot result in the public claim stage. Plan accordingly—don’t rely on post-shot deception as a tactic.

When selecting a fire cell against a target, favor central cells (4–6) in early and mid rounds to maximize probability of overlap with others’ hides. In late or decisive rounds, bias toward cells I have actually used previously if I suspect opponents are matching my pattern; if I deviate from the standing order to hit a leader or Harbor, choose the cell most consistent with where I expect them given their prior behavior.

Use the feedback of hit/miss (my private result and observed others’ claims) to update a mental map of opponents’ preferred cells and tendencies. If an opponent repeatedly hits or misses a given target, infer their likely fire cells and whether they are reusing hides; adjust my hides to exploit predictable targeting. Conversely, if I see a string of hits on a given opponent from others, assume they are being targeted more and consider changing hides to reduce being a convenient target.

Escort claims: only name an escorted boat when I expect credible mutual naming that will result in the 5-point mutual payoff. Do not make one-sided escort claims for signaling or vanity—there is no benefit. Use notes to try to coordinate a reciprocal claim earlier in the patrol if I want those points; if coordination fails, default to salvage: none.

When considering firing on Harbor, account for the enforced transfer: firing on Harbor immediately shifts 3 points from Harbor to me regardless of whether the shot hits. Attack Harbor only if (a) the 3-point transfer plus the strategic benefits (removing the payroll-holder’s deterrent) are worth the likely retaliation, or (b) I am behind late and need a guaranteed points swing to change standings. If I am ahead, avoid attacking Harbor to prevent giving leaders motivation to retaliate and to preserve stability.

When behind late in the patrol, I should accept higher-risk plays: deviate from formation, consider attacking leaders or Harbor, and use my hide placement to try to be in the right cell to take a hit where it yields the most swing. These moves are justified when the expected value in points gained outweighs the additional exposure or retaliation risk.

When ahead late in the patrol, reduce risk: stick to standing order targets, conservative hides (consistent with minimizing being hit), truthful claims (as required), and avoid creating reasons for others to concentrate fire on me.

Do not rely on deception through false fire claims—the rules enforce truth in claims. Instead, use timing, hide pattern changes, and selective deviations to create ambiguity in opponents’ expectations.

If opponents’ public claims or patterns become inconsistent with each other, mark those players as unreliable partners for escort coordination and avoid offering reciprocal escorts to them; punish only if I can do so profitably (i.e., the retaliation or removal produces a net point gain or protects my position).

If I attempt a risky or deceptive maneuver and it is exposed or leads to a net loss, revert to truthful, conservative play for the remainder of the patrol and focus on maximizing expected points given my standing.

When I have no information about others’ escort intentions, default to salvage: none. Only invest effort in arranging mutual escorts when there is evidence of willingness to reciprocate (notes, prior mutual behavior).

Keep the above framework flexible: constantly update hide choices, fire targets, and escort plans based on scoreline, remaining rounds, and observed behavior.
